Field surveys of the Zambezi happy, Pharyngochromis darlingi, a cichlid endemic to the lower Zambezi River system, have provided detailed life-history data. Adult individuals attain a maximum total length of 22 centimeters [Li = 22 centimeters], a size that positions this species as a medium-bodied cichlid within its regional assemblage. The length at which puberty begins, marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence in males and vitellogenesis in females, has been recorded at 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters]. This threshold is not abrupt; rather, transitional individuals between 9 and 11 centimeters show intermediate stages of gametogenesis. The wet weight corresponding to this pubertal length, derived from length-weight regressions for the species, is approximately 12.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 12.9 grams], a value that lies between the minimal larval mass and the adult maximum, illustrating the substantial somatic investment needed before reproductive activation. These morphometric benchmarks are essential for distinguishing immature, rapidly growing juveniles from the adult population that contributes to annual recruitment.

Reproductive output in P. darlingi has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce 200 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 200 eggs per spawning event], with approximately one spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event occurring each year]. This level of fecundity is typical for a maternal mouthbrooding cichlid of moderate body size, where brood size is heavily constrained by buccal cavity volume. The continuous spawning pattern observed distinguishes this species from congeneric forms that exhibit more pronounced seasonal breeding peaks tied to flood pulses in the natural riverine habitat.

Egg diameter measurements indicate that the wet weight of a newly emerged yolk-sac larva is very small, approximately 0.0082 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0082 grams]. This mass corresponds to an average egg diameter of 2.5 millimeters, as determined from preserved clutches. The lecithotrophic alevin relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first days post-eclosion, with the mouth remaining closed until yolk-sac resorption is nearly complete. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs when the larva reaches a precarious trophic switch, and the small size of the hatchling makes it especially vulnerable to starvation if suitable planktonic prey is not immediately available. In the riverine environment, synchrony between hatching events and zooplankton blooms is therefore likely critical for first-feeding survival.

Maximum adult body size in P. darlingi corresponds to an ultimate wet weight estimated at 133 grams [Wwi = 133 grams] for the largest individuals captured during systematic gill-net sampling. This asymptotic mass is consistent with predictions from the species length-weight relationship of 0.01413 times length raised to the 2.96 power, indicating near-isometric scaling. Females typically reach this maximum mass only after multiple spawning seasons, as the energetic demands of mouthbrooding impose a trade-off between somatic growth and current reproductive effort. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that the 133-gram ceiling is close to the upper limit for maternal mouthbrooders in the genus, reflecting constraints imposed by branchial basket volume and metabolic capacity during the protracted buccal incubation period.

Longevity records for P. darlingi, obtained from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Zambezi River floodplain at an average water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] under natural conditions. This corresponds to approximately eight years, a moderately long lifespan for a cichlid of its size and comparable to that reported for other maternal mouthbrooding cichlids in the African Rift lakes. The extended lifespan likely reflects a bet-hedging strategy in an environment where annual recruitment success is highly variable due to unpredictable flood regimes. Older individuals may buffer population persistence during sequences of poor reproductive years, underscoring the demographic importance of the adult stage in this species.
